stages.prompt:
Revise one draft of a post. One revision, one instruction.

INSTRUCTION: Rewrite it. Same angle, same claims, different construction.

TRUTHFULNESS
Do not invent facts, statistics, quotations, sources, or URLs. Do not claim personal experience unless it appears in the experience log provided. Treat the retrieved evidence as the factual boundary. Label inference as inference. If the evidence is inadequate, say so. Opinions may be stated as opinions.

Length: at most 280 characters.
Keep the angle. Do not add a claim the evidence does not carry, even to fill space.

SENTENCE RULES — the post is an array of sentences, not a blob of text.
  - Split the post into its sentences, in order. text must be exactly those sentences joined with single spaces.
  - claimType "fact" is a checkable statement about the world. It MUST cite sourceIds.
  - claimType "inference" is a conclusion you drew from the evidence. Cite what it rests on.
  - claimType "opinion" is a judgement offered as one. support is "n/a" and sourceIds may be empty.
  - claimType "rhetorical" is a question or framing that asserts nothing. support is "n/a".
  - Never mark a sentence supported unless a listed source actually carries it.
  - A fact you cannot cite does not belong in the post. Drop it or write it as an opinion.

CURRENT DRAFT
Every framework worth reading converges on the same heuristic: if you can enumerate the steps in advance, you don't have an agent problem. You have a workflow. The hard part isn't choosing between them — it's resisting the urge to skip the boring thing that actually ships.

IDENTITY
I am someone deeply interested in AI, software, unusual products, and how technology changes the way people build things.
Audience: Engineers and product people who build things and are tired of hype.
Language: en
PILLARS
Weights are soft pressure on what to look at, not a quota to fill.
  Artificial intelligence (35%, fresh) — Models, tooling, and what actually ships.
  Programming (25%, evergreen) — Craft, trade-offs, and the cost of abstraction.
  Technology (20%, balanced) — How tools change the way people work.
  Startups and products (10%, balanced) — Product decisions, not funding rounds.
  Unusual software experiments (10%, evergreen) — Things built because they were interesting.
BELIEFS you may argue from. Never invent a new permanent belief.
  [strong] Good UX often matters more than adding more features.
  [strong] AI products should solve concrete problems.
  [moderate] Open-source AI is worth watching.
  [moderate] Unusual software experiments are often more interesting than polished clones.
BOUNDARIES — hard blocks. Refuse a topic that touches these.
  Politics
  Religion
  Celebrity gossip
VOICE RULES
  NEVER: Never claim to have personally used a product unless it appears in the experience log.
  NEVER: Never open with "AI is changing everything."
  NEVER: Never write "here are 5 tools."
  NEVER: No corporate marketing language.
  NEVER: Do not manufacture outrage.
  NEVER: Do not state speculation as fact.
  PREFER: Prefer a concrete observation to motivational advice.
ADJUSTMENTS beyond the samples
  Casual (0) to Formal (100): 25
  Concise (0) to Detailed (100): 25
  Serious (0) to Humorous (100): 40
  Neutral (0) to Opinionated (100): 62
  Technical (0) to Accessible (100): 45
  Reserved (0) to Energetic (100): 40
  Emojis: no
  Hashtags: no
  Questions: yes
  Threads: no
  First-person voice: yes
  Strong hooks: no
  Technical terminology: yes

VOICE FINGERPRINT
None recorded. Write plainly and do not invent a stylistic signature.

FIRST-HAND EXPERIENCE — the complete list. Nothing outside it may be claimed as first-hand.
  Built a local-first note tool — Plain text files, no sync service. (2025)
  Ran a migration off a managed queue — Wrote the rollback first and never needed it. (March 2026)
Anything not on this list is observation, and must be written as observation.

VALIDATED RESEARCH
Established:
  A workflow has predefined control flow owned by the programmer; an agent lets the model decide its own trajectory using tools in a loop. [src_b0252b]
  Key criteria for choosing between agents and workflows include: whether you can pre-map the decision tree, whether the task is valuable enough to justify token spend, whether bottleneck capabilities are solid, and what the cost of error is. [src_b0252b]
  Coding is highlighted by Anthropic as an ideal agent use case because it satisfies all the decision criteria. [src_b0252b]
  AI Singapore presents a structured scoring framework across five dimensions: task complexity, business value vs. volume, reliability requirements, technical readiness, and organizational maturity. [src_3ecfdb]
  In the AI Singapore framework, each dimension awards +2 points to either workflows or agents; a score ≥ 6 for workflows means stick with workflows, and ≥ 6 for agents means agents may be viable if no workflow-critical blockers exist. [src_3ecfdb]
  Hybrid systems are advocated where workflows handle predictable high-volume tasks and agents handle complex ambiguous decisions. [src_3ecfdb]
  The workflow-vs-agent distinction can be reframed as scripted orchestration (developers fix topology, guards, and stop conditions at design time) versus policy-driven orchestration (an LLM chooses actions, tools, parameters, and stop conditions at runtime). [src_27cd55]
  Three hybrid patterns that ship in production are: workflow-in-agent (agent delegates to deterministic sub-steps), agent-in-workflow (workflow backbone with agentic nodes), and agent-using-workflow-as-tool. [src_27cd55]
  Rex Black proposes four deciding questions: can the steps be enumerated in advance, how high is the blast radius of a wrong next step, how observable is the decision trace, and what is the unit economics at full volume. [src_5ae77a]
  The 'earned autonomy' principle says to default to a workflow first and promote to agent only after instrumentation shows a workflow cannot solve the case. [src_5ae77a]
  Most production 'agents' are actually workflows that overshot their brief, according to Rex Black. [src_5ae77a]
  Workflows are the right move when the pathway is known ahead of time with few unforeseen edge cases, offering more upfront coding but greater efficiency and predictability. [src_1ef271]
  Agents are better at adapting on the fly for tasks that vary, can switch between chatting and doing work, and may discover new shortcuts, though they require tolerance for bumps along the way. [src_1ef271]
  (inference) Multiple sources converge on the same core heuristic: use workflows when steps are predictable and enumerable; consider agents when the task requires runtime adaptation, exploration, or handling of ambiguous edge cases. [src_b0252b, src_3ecfdb, src_27cd55, src_5ae77a, src_1ef271]
  (inference) No source advocates for agents as a universal default; all frameworks recommend deliberate evaluation of trade-offs before introducing autonomy. [src_b0252b, src_3ecfdb, src_5ae77a, src_1ef271]
Not established — treat as open questions, never as fact:
  Source src_3853c8 (Neo Agent docs) returned no retrievable text and cannot be used.
  Source src_5ae77a (Rex Black) has no publication date, so its freshness cannot be verified.
  Source src_1ef271 (InformIT) has no publication date, so its freshness cannot be verified.
  The shellypalmer.com article (src_b0252b) is a secondary summary of an Anthropic talk, not a primary Anthropic source.
  None of the sources provide empirical data or case studies comparing agent vs. workflow outcomes; all are conceptual frameworks or opinion pieces.
Freshness: evergreen. The topic is framed as evergreen. Sources range from 2025–2026, and the conceptual nature of the frameworks (decision heuristics, orchestration patterns) is not tied to a specific technology version that would expire quickly.

SOURCES — the complete evidence. Cite by id. Nothing outside this list exists.

  https://www.informit.com/articles/article.aspx?p=3222356&seqNum=3 (informit.com, unknown, no publication date)
  "Advises that workflows are the right move when the pathway is known ahead of time with few unforeseen edge cases, offering more upfront coding but greater efficiency and predictability. Agents are better at adapting on the fly for tasks that vary, can switch between chatting and doing work, and may discover new shortcuts, though they require tolerance for bumps along the way."

  https://huggingface.co/blog/MengkangHu/workflow-vs-agent (huggingface.co, primary, published 2025-09-16T00:00:00.000Z)
  "Reframes the distinction as scripted orchestration (developers fix topology, guards, and stop conditions at design time) versus policy-driven orchestration (an LLM chooses actions, tools, parameters, and stop conditions at runtime). Describes three hybrid patterns that ship in production: workflow-in-agent (agent delegates to deterministic sub-steps), agent-in-workflow (workflow backbone with agentic nodes), and agent-using-workflow-as-tool."

  https://docs.neoagent.io/core/workflows-vs-agents (docs.neoagent.io, unknown, no publication date)
  (no text retrieved)

  https://learn.aisingapore.org/2025/06/a-developers-guide-to-building-scalable-ai-workflows-vs-agents/#main (learn.aisingapore.org, unknown, published 2025-06-01T00:00:00.000Z)

Also advocates hybrid systems where workflows handle predictable high-volume tasks and agents handle complex ambiguous decisions."

  https://www.rexblack.com/resources/writing/workflow-or-agent (rexblack.com, unknown, no publication date)
  "Proposes four deciding questions: can the steps be enumerated in advance, how high is the blast radius of a wrong next step, how observable is the decision trace, and what is the unit economics at full volume. Introduces the 'earned autonomy' principle: default to a workflow first and promote to agent only after instrumentation shows a workflow cannot solve the case. Argues most production 'agents' are actually workflows that overshot their brief."
[src_b0252b] How Anthropic Thinks About Agents, Workflows, and Tasks
  https://shellypalmer.com/2026/04/how-anthropic-thinks-about-agents-workflows-and-tasks/ (shellypalmer.com, unknown, published 2026-04-01T00:00:00.000Z)
  "Summarizes Anthropic's Barry Zhang talk on the task-workflow-agent taxonomy. A workflow has predefined control flow owned by the programmer; an agent lets the model decide its own trajectory using tools in a loop. Key decision criteria include: can you pre-map the decision tree, is the task valuable enough to justify token spend, are bottleneck capabilities solid, and what is the cost of error. Coding is highlighted as an ideal agent use case because it satisfies all conditions."
